edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of military service, you are held by a bridle. Then begin to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, because labor with arms is imminent. To the command of the King, obedience is to be given with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times joyful. He, a good soldier, always expects things to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, completely send away idleness, so that you may be present daily to your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signals at dawn. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the King, to see the soldier prepared; the King is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts, he, joyful for victory, suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be. You, moreover, do not spare yourself in respect to Belial: be more energetic, so that he may give fame in exchange for death.

pass_b_english: Once you've enlisted in God's service, you're under discipline. It's time to leave your old ways behind - a life of luxury won't cut it when you're facing the hard work of spiritual warfare. To obey the King's commands with all your heart is crucial if you hope to make it through the tough times ahead with joy. A good soldier is always on the lookout for what's to come, so don't get complacent and don't let idleness creep in - be ready to serve your Commander every day. Get a head start by being prepared beforehand and reviewing your marching orders at dawn. When you see battle looming, prepare yourself for the intense struggle ahead. The King's glory is in having a soldier who's ready for action, and He's present with us, ready to give us victory and fulfill our hopes. He's preparing rewards for us, and He's joyful when we win - He even assigns a personal attendant to us. Meanwhile, don't go easy on yourself when it comes to resisting Belial - be more energetic and motivated, so that even if it costs you your life, you'll gain fame and recognition.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant theological expansions and interpretive shifts not present in the Latin source. 1. 'Militiae nomen cum dederis' (When you have given the name of military service) is rendered as 'Once you've enlisted in God's service', adding 'God's' which is not in the text. 2. 'labor imminet armis' (labor with arms is imminent) is rendered as 'facing the hard work of spiritual warfare', adding 'spiritual'. 3. 'optato propter spem dominicaturum' (who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope) is rendered as 'ready to give us victory and fulfill our hopes', which changes the grammatical structure and meaning. 4. 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' (He suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be) is rendered as 'He's joyful when we win - He even assigns a personal attendant to us', which is a complete departure from the literal sense of the Latin.
reasons: Pass B adds 'God's' to 'militiae' and 'spiritual' to 'armis' which are not in the Latin. Pass B renders 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' as 'He's joyful when we win - He even assigns a personal attendant to us', which fails to preserve the sense of the Latin verbs and structure.

review.notes: The Latin text is correctly identified as 'Instructions LIII' from the specified edition. The translation preserves the original meaning, including the correct use of terms like 'militiae' as 'military service' and 'freno' as 'bridle'. The scripture citations are not present in the text, so no issues arise from that. The title 'The Good Soldier' accurately reflects the content of the passage.
